name: Jelena Dokic
milestone_by_age_26: Won the US Open girls' singles title in 1998 at age 15 and ended the year as world No. 1 in the junior singles rankings.
early_history_summary: Started playing tennis at age 5-6 after her father saw Monica Seles on television. Family emigrated from Yugoslavia to Australia in 1994. She held an Australian Institute of Sport scholarship and won the US Open girls' title at 15, then made a stunning Wimbledon quarterfinal run at 16 in 1999, defeating world No. 1 Martina Hingis.
family_context_summary: Born to a Serb father and Croat mother in Osijek, Yugoslavia; family emigrated to Australia in 1994. Father Damir was intensely involved in her tennis but was also physically abusive, controlling her career and taking her winnings.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father introduced her to tennis after seeing Monica Seles on television and coached her intensively from age 5-6, though his involvement was abusive rather than pedagogically constructive.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Australian Institute of Sport, early specialization, abusive father-coach, immigration
evidence_summary: Dokic started tennis at age 5-6 under her father's intense coaching after the family emigrated from Yugoslavia to Australia. She held an Australian Institute of Sport scholarship and won the US Open girls' title at 15, becoming junior world No. 1. Her father's involvement was abusive rather than constructive, and the family had limited financial resources. Her Wimbledon quarterfinal at 16, where she defeated world No. 1 Hingis, demonstrated exceptional early talent.
starting_point: Born to a working-class Serb-Croat family in Osijek, Yugoslavia; father was an amateur tennis coach who became abusive, mother was a homemaker; family emigrated to Australia in 1994.
current_position: Retired from professional tennis in 2014; works as a tennis commentator and mental health advocate; resides in Australia.

trajectory.event: Won US Open girls' singles title and ended the year as world No. 1 in junior singles rankings.
Reached Wimbledon quarterfinals as a qualifier, defeating world No. 1 Martina Hingis in the first round.
Won first WTA singles title at the Rome Masters (Italian Open), defeating Amelie Mauresmo in the final.
Reached career-high singles ranking of world No. 4.
Made a comeback to reach the Australian Open quarterfinals, returning to the top 100.
Retired from professional tennis with 6 WTA singles titles and a career-high ranking of No. 4.

name: P. V. Sindhu
milestone_by_age_26: Won bronze at the 2013 BWF World Championships at age 18, becoming India's first medallist in women's singles at the World Championships.
early_history_summary: Started playing badminton at age 8, inspired by Pullela Gopichand's All England Open triumph. Joined Gopichand's Badminton Academy in Hyderabad, traveling 25-56km daily for training. Won multiple junior national titles and broke into the BWF top 20 at age 17 in 2012.
family_context_summary: Born to a family of athletes in Hyderabad; both parents were national-level volleyball players, and her father Ramana won bronze at the 1986 Seoul Asian Games and received the Arjuna Award in 2000.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were national-level volleyball players, providing an athletic family environment and understanding of competitive sport, though not badminton-specific expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Gopichand Academy, athletic family, early specialization, daily training commute
evidence_summary: Sindhu grew up in a sports family in Hyderabad with both parents being national-level volleyball players. She started badminton at age 8 and joined the elite Gopichand Badminton Academy, traveling 25-56km daily for training. She won multiple junior national titles and broke into the BWF top 20 at 17. Her bronze at the 2013 World Championships at 18 made her India's first women's singles World Championship medallist.
starting_point: Born into a sports-oriented family in Hyderabad, India; both parents were national-level volleyball players, with father Ramana an Asian Games bronze medallist and Arjuna Award recipient.
current_position: Active professional badminton player; career-high world ranking No. 2 (2017); two-time Olympic medallist (silver 2016, bronze 2020); 2019 World Champion; current world ranking approximately No. 10.

trajectory.event: Broke into the BWF World Rankings top 20 and won gold at the Asian Junior Championships.
Won bronze at the BWF World Championships, becoming India's first women's singles World Championship medallist.
Won Olympic silver medal at the Rio Olympics, becoming the first Indian badminton player to reach an Olympic final.
Achieved career-high world ranking of No. 2 in April 2017.
Won gold at the BWF World Championships, becoming the first Indian to become badminton world champion.
Won Olympic bronze medal at the Tokyo Olympics, becoming the first Indian woman to win two Olympic medals.

name: A. R. Penck
milestone_by_age_26: No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 found. Founded an informal artist group at 14 but was rejected from art academies and the official artists' association; his Standart series and international recognition came after age 27.
early_history_summary: Took painting lessons with Jurgen Bottcher as a teenager in Dresden and founded the informal artist group Erste Phalanx Nedserd at 14. Was rejected from art academies and worked as a draftsman, stoker, and night watchman while making art independently in East Germany.
evidence_summary: Penck took art lessons as a teenager in Dresden and founded an informal artist group at 14, but was rejected from official art academies and the GDR artists' association. He worked menial jobs while making art independently. His Standart series and first real recognition came in the late 1960s, after age 27, and he was eventually stripped of citizenship and deported to the West in 1980.

name: Mahsa Amini
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Amini was an ordinary young woman who died in police custody at age 22, becoming an involuntary icon of the Iranian protest movement. She had no personal achievements in any domain.
early_history_summary: Born to a Kurdish family in Saqqez, Iran. Attended secondary school and aspired to become a doctor. Had recently been admitted to university in Urmia to study biology when she was arrested by Iran's morality police in September 2022 and died in custody three days later.
family_context_summary: Born to a Kurdish family in Saqqez, Kurdistan Province, Iran. Her family was ordinary; she had a younger brother named Ashkan.
evidence_summary: Amini was an ordinary Kurdish-Iranian woman with no notable personal achievements. She died in police custody at 22, and her death became a catalyst for nationwide protests. She is an involuntary symbol rather than an achiever in any domain.

name: Chris de Burgh
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Signed to A&M Records in October 1974 at age 26 and debut album was released in February 1975, but the album failed to chart. His breakthrough hit 'The Lady in Red' came in 1986 at age 38.

family_context_summary: Born in Argentina to British parents who traveled extensively; family bought Bargy Castle in Ireland when he was 12. Father was a British diplomat and mother was of English descent. Family was middle-to-upper class.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Parents were not musicians but supported his musical ambitions.
evidence_summary: De Burgh grew up in Bargy Castle in Ireland and developed performing skills entertaining castle guests. He signed with A&M Records in 1974 at age 26 and released his debut album in early 1975, but it failed to chart. His major success came much later with 'The Lady in Red' in 1986 at age 38. No material milestone by age 26 was identified.

name: Bent Larsen
milestone_by_age_26: Became an International Master at age 19 in 1954 with a bronze medal at the Amsterdam Olympiad, and won his first Danish Championship the same year. Became a Grandmaster at 21 in 1956.
early_history_summary: Discovered chess at age 7 during a bout of childhood illnesses. Began playing seriously at 17 when he moved to Copenhagen to study civil engineering, but dropped out to play chess professionally. Won the Danish Championship and became International Master at 19 in 1954, then Grandmaster at 21 in 1956.
family_context_summary: Born in Tilsted, near Thisted in rural Denmark. Father knew chess but was not a serious player. Family moved to Holstebro and later Aalborg during his childhood.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father knew the game of chess casually but had no domain expertise or professional chess background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught, Copenhagen chess scene, Danish championship, childhood illness discovery
evidence_summary: Larsen discovered chess at age 7 during childhood illnesses and learned the game from another boy and his father. He was not considered a prodigy, but began playing seriously at 17 when he moved to Copenhagen for engineering studies. He dropped out to pursue chess professionally, won the Danish Championship and became International Master at 19 in 1954, and Grandmaster at 21 in 1956. He studied Russian during military service to read chess literature, showing deep self-directed dedication.
starting_point: Born in a small town in rural Denmark; father knew chess casually but had no professional background; family moved several times during his childhood.
current_position: Died in 2010 at age 75 in Buenos Aires, Argentina; final status: retired chess grandmaster and author, six-time Danish Champion, four-time World Championship Candidate.

trajectory.event: Became International Master with bronze medal at the Amsterdam Olympiad and won his first Danish Championship.
Became International Grandmaster with gold-medal performance on board one at the Moscow Olympiad, drawing with World Champion Botvinnik.
Won the prestigious Havana tournament ahead of multiple world-class players, establishing himself as a top contender.
Reached peak ranking of No. 4 in the world and lost to Bobby Fischer in the Candidates Tournament semifinal.
Died of a cerebral hemorrhage in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

name: Momcilo Perisic
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Graduated from the Ground Forces Military Academy in 1966 at age 22 and was a junior officer in the Yugoslav People's Army. His major milestone as Chief of the General Staff came in 1993 at age 49.
early_history_summary: Born in Kostunici, German-occupied Serbia. Graduated from the Ground Forces Military Academy in 1966 and joined the Yugoslav People's Army as a career officer. Progressed through military ranks over decades before becoming Chief of the General Staff in 1993.
evidence_summary: Perisic graduated from the military academy at 22 and served as a junior officer in the Yugoslav People's Army. By age 26 he was a young officer with no notable achievements. His career milestones came much later: commander of the 13th Corps in 1992 and Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army in 1993 at age 49. He was later indicted by the ICTY and acquitted on appeal in 2013.

family_context_summary: Born in Pamplona to a Navarrese family. Not documented in reviewed sources.

name: Vladimir Lyakhov
milestone_by_age_26: Selected as a Soviet cosmonaut on 5 May 1967 at age 25, chosen from thousands of military pilots for one of the most elite programs in the world.
early_history_summary: Born in Antratsyt, Ukrainian SSR. Graduated from the Military Higher School of Pilots in Chuguyev in 1964. Served as a military pilot in the Soviet Air Force. Selected as a cosmonaut in May 1967 as part of the TsPK-4 group, undergoing basic cosmonaut training from 1967 to 1969.
family_context_summary: Born in Antratsyt, Ukrainian SSR, Soviet Union. Not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet military aviation, cosmonaut selection, Air Force Group 4
evidence_summary: Lyakhov graduated from the Military Higher School of Pilots in 1964 and served as a Soviet Air Force pilot. He was selected as a cosmonaut on 5 May 1967 at age 25, chosen from thousands of candidates for the elite Soviet space program. His basic cosmonaut training lasted from 1967 to 1969. His first actual space flight came much later in 1979 at age 37, but cosmonaut selection itself was a major career milestone in the Soviet military-space hierarchy.
starting_point: Born in Antratsyt, Ukrainian SSR, Soviet Union; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died on 19 April 2018 at age 76 in Astrakhan, Russia; final status: retired cosmonaut, twice Hero of the Soviet Union, spent 333 days in space across three missions.

trajectory.event: Selected as a Soviet cosmonaut as part of Air Force Group 4 (TsPK-4), chosen from thousands of military pilots.
Commanded Soyuz 32 to Salyut-6, setting a space endurance record of 175 days with Valeri Ryumin.
Commanded Soyuz T-9 to Salyut-7, spending 149 days in space and conducting two spacewalks.
Commanded Soyuz TM-6 to Mir space station, spending 8 days in space with Abdul Ahad Mohmand.
Died on 19 April 2018 in Astrakhan, Russia.

name: Ruud Krol
milestone_by_age_26: Became a regular starter at Ajax Amsterdam in the 1969-70 season at age 20 and made his debut for the Netherlands national team the same year. Went on to win three consecutive European Cups with Ajax (1971-73).
early_history_summary: Born in Amsterdam. Joined Ajax as a youth and broke into the first team in the 1968-69 season. Became a regular in 1969-70 after the departure of left-back Theo van Duivenbode. Made his Netherlands national team debut in 1969 at age 20. Was part of the legendary Ajax team that won three consecutive European Cups under Rinus Michels and Stefan Kovacs.
family_context_summary: Born in Amsterdam, Netherlands. Not documented in reviewed sources regarding family financial status or background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Ajax academy, Total Football, Amsterdam, Rinus Michels, Johan Cruyff
evidence_summary: Krol was born in Amsterdam and joined Ajax, one of the world's premier football clubs, as a youth player. He became a first-team regular at 20 under manager Rinus Michels and made his Netherlands debut the same year. He was part of the legendary Ajax team that won three consecutive European Cups (1971-73), though he missed the 1971 final with a broken leg. His development was accelerated by immersion in the Total Football revolution at Ajax alongside Johan Cruyff and under Michels' guidance.
starting_point: Born in Amsterdam, Netherlands; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Retired from playing in 1986; former Dutch international (83 caps); regarded as one of the greatest defenders of all time; has had a long managerial career across multiple countries; resides in the Netherlands.

Reached the FIFA World Cup final with the Netherlands, named to the All-Star Team.

family_context_summary: Born in Budapest, Hungary. Family background before marriage not documented in reviewed sources.
